newsitem.title: UK: Chile's Frei vows to tackle poverty, infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Frei vows to tackle poverty, infrastructure.

text.p: Chile said on Monday its economic success over the past six years gave it a fighting chance of overcoming extreme poverty, while tackling its inadequate infrastructure will be the next issue to top the agenda.

Speaking to company chiefs and financiers during an official visit to Britain, Chile's President Eduardo Frei said his country had established a firm base for social progress after achieving annual average growth of 7.0 percent since 1990.
"This promising framework allows us to achieve to a greater extent our task of constructing a more equal society and defeating poverty," he said.

"Chile can not aspire to be a modern, stable and developed country if it does not use the necessary will and imagination to make growth compatible with equality, development with solidarity, and progress with the defeat of poverty," he added.

Chile boasts one of the most successful economies of Latin America. Its growth rate is the fastest in the western hemisphere and it is one of the few Latin American nations to have won an investment grade credit rating.
But a report by the U.S. Development Programme recently likened the gap between Chile's rich and poor to that between Canada and Ghana.
Frei however said the situation had been steadily improving.
With wages and productivity increasing at around 4.0 percent annually since 1990, he said purchasing power had risen on average by 26 percent, more than during the whole of the 1980s.

Meanwhile a network of bilateral agreements across Latin America, and in particular Chile's association agreement with regional trade group Mercosur, provided the impetus for a concerted programme of infrastructure development.
"This will begin with investments between Chile and Argentina for more than $320 million in constructing access roads and priority border passes," Frei said.
Building connections between the Pacific and the Atlantic oceans were a priority, while investment in public infrastructure was increasing dramatically.

"These decisions will rapidly transform the face of our country in the forthcoming years in essential areas of our development, such as ports, airports, urban and intercity roads, railways and energy," he said.
Frei also pointed to the success of Chile's five-year-old free trade agreement with Mexico, adding he hoped a similar accord would be signed with Canada soon.
Association with the North American free trade body (Nafta), comprising Canada, the United States and Mexico, was a priority.
"We are confident that when certain problems beyond our control are resolved, we will begin the relevant negotiations," he said.

Agreement with Nafta stalled last year when the United States declined to give Chile the "fast track" authority that would have effectively prevented it from having to negotiate twice -- with the U.S. government and with Congress.
Negotiations are on hold until after the U.S. elections.

Chile itself holds nationwide municipal elections on October 27. These are considered a crucial political test for Frei, who took office for a six-year presidential term in 1994. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
